arXiv:2603.26025v1 [cond-mat.soft] 27 Mar 2026

Spontaneous oscillations and geometric cutoff in confined bacterial swarms

Bing Miao Affiliation: Center of Materials Science and Optoelectronics Engineering, College of Materials Science and Opto-Electronic Technology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (UCAS), Beijing 100049, China    Lei-Han Tang Email: tangleihan@westlake.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Physics, Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, Hong Kong SAR, China Affiliation: Center for Interdisciplinary Studies, Westlake University, Hangzhou, China
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Self-organized dynamic patterns in dense active matter are striking manifestations of non-equilibrium physics. A prominent example is the macroscopic elliptical motion observed in quasi-2D bacterial suspensions, which has lacked a physical explanation. Here, we examine a minimal linear response framework coupling bacterial swimming dynamics with fluid flow, treating long-range hydrodynamic interactions as a macroscopic communication channel. We demonstrate that microscopic swim motion, via Jeffery coupling, manifests as a “phase-leading” response to local shear flows. System-wide sustained oscillations, on the other hand, require both a critical bacterial density and strict geometric confinement. By analytically predicting the onset cell density and maximum film thickness, our model achieves excellent quantitative agreement with experiments, establishing a unified physical framework for self-organized periodic motion of elongated body in active fluids.

Introduction — Active fluids are fundamentally characterized by the continuous injection of energy at the scale of their individual constituents, driving them far from thermodynamic equilibrium.[1, 2, 3] In bacterial suspensions, for instance, this localized energy injection manifests through the persistent, run-and-tumble swimming dynamics of individual cells.[4, 5, 6] A central theme in the statistical mechanics of active matter is how these microscopic, non-equilibrium activities translate into macroscopic fluid behavior.[7, 8, 9] At sufficiently large spatial and temporal scales, the complex trajectories of individual agents typically coarse-grain: the persistent motion of bacteria randomizes over many tumbling events, renormalizing into effective passive properties such as enhanced translational diffusion or altered viscosity.[10] In such a scenario, the active fluid often loses its distinct non-equilibrium signature, phenomenologically mimicking a passive, equilibrium-like continuous medium.[11]

However, this macroscopic passive limit can be destabilized when individual cells communicate. A prominent example is the collective, elliptical motion of active bacteria observed above a critical cell density in a thin liquid film of 5 to 10 μ\mum thickness[12] (see Fig. 1). Even at high cell volume fractions of approximately 20%20\%, individual bacteria maintain their characteristic run-and-tumble motion with an effective tumbling rate. While a 2D effective model can reproduce the synchronized trajectories through prescribed angular couplings[12], it leaves the physical origin of these interactions unresolved.

In this Letter, we move beyond phenomenological descriptions to establish a first-principles hydrodynamic theory. Building on a recently formulated response-function framework[13], we model the bacterial population as active agents that interact and communicate via the embedding fluid. In this view, macroscopic spontaneous oscillations emerge when the gain from cellular signal relay overcomes environmental dissipation—requiring both a collective “phase-leading” response and sufficient cell density. We demonstrate that these emergent oscillations do not require explicit behavioral programming; rather, they arise naturally as a rigorous consequence of long-range hydrodynamic interactions, governed by active stress generation and the Jeffery torque in a statistical sense. Furthermore, by explicitly incorporating the vertical boundary conditions of the experimental setup, our framework reveals that strict geometric confinement—specifically, the fluid film thickness—is not merely a secondary boundary effect, but the fundamental control parameter dictating the onset of instability.

The model — We begin by establishing the coupled dynamic equations for the bacteria and the fluid. The time evolution of the orientation-resolved single-particle distribution function ρ⁡(r→,p→,t)\rho(\vec{r},\vec{p},t), where the state of a bacterium is characterized by its position r→\vec{r} and unit orientation vector p→\vec{p}, is governed by a Smoluchowski equation representing conservation of probability [14]:

∂tρ⁡(r→,p→,t)=−[∇⋅𝐉T​(r→,p→,t)+∇p→⋅𝐉R​(r→,p→,t)].\partial_{t}\rho(\vec{r},\vec{p},t)=-[\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}_{\rm T}(\vec{r},\vec{p},t)+\nabla_{\vec{p}}\cdot\mathbf{J}_{\rm R}(\vec{r},\vec{p},t)]. (1)

Here, 𝐉T\mathbf{J}_{\rm T} and 𝐉R\mathbf{J}_{\rm R} denote the translational and rotational fluxes, respectively defined as:

𝐉T\displaystyle\mathbf{J}_{\rm T} =\displaystyle= ρ𝐕T=ρ[vsp→+u→−DT∇lnρ],\displaystyle\rho\mathbf{V}_{\rm T}=\rho[v_{\rm s}\vec{p}+\vec{u}-D_{\rm T}\nabla\ln\rho],
𝐉R\displaystyle\mathbf{J}_{\rm R} =\displaystyle= ρ​𝐕R=ρ⁡[(𝐈−p→​p→)⋅∇u→⋅p→−DR​∇p→​ln⁡ρ].\displaystyle\rho\mathbf{V}_{\rm R}=\rho[(\mathbf{I}-\vec{p}\vec{p})\cdot\nabla\vec{u}\cdot\vec{p}-D_{R}\nabla_{\vec{p}}\ln\rho].

The effective velocities 𝐕T\mathbf{V}_{\rm T} and 𝐕R\mathbf{V}_{\rm R} are composed of deterministic drift and stochastic diffusion. In the translational flux, vsv_{\rm s} represents the intrinsic swimming speed of the bacterium, while u→​(r→)\vec{u}(\vec{r}) is the local fluid velocity field that advects the cells. In the rotational flux, the drift term corresponds to the Jeffery equation for a rod-shaped particle in a shear flow [15], where 𝐈\mathbf{I} is the identity tensor. Finally, DTD_{\rm T} and DRD_{\rm R} are the translational and rotational diffusion coefficients, respectively; these characterize the stochastic components of bacterial motion and can be determined via single-bacterium trajectory experiments.[5]

The fluid flow field is governed by the Stokes equation:

Here, we have assumed a low Reynolds number regime where inertia is negligible, resulting in an instantaneous force-balance equation, with μ\mu the fluid viscosity and 𝚺⁡(r→,t)\mathbf{\Sigma}(\vec{r},t) the active stress tensor exerted on the fluid by the swimming bacteria. The latter is defined as the orientational average of individual force dipoles,

To align with the experimental setup illustrated in Fig. 1, we shall focus on laminar shear flow

Linear response in multipole expansion — Assuming the flow field u±​(z,t)u_{\pm}(z,t) is weak, we treat the right-hand-side of Eq. (3) as perturbations to the static solution. As usually done, we proceed by expanding the density distribution into spherical harmonics:

ρ⁡(z,θ,ϕ,t)=∑l,mal​m​(z,t)​Ylm​(θ,ϕ).\rho(z,\theta,\phi,t)=\sum_{l,m}a_{lm}(z,t)Y_{l}^{m}(\theta,\phi). (5)

In this representation, the active stress driving the fluid in Eq. (4) is governed exclusively by the off-diagonal nematic order parameter, a2,±1a_{2,\pm 1}. As a direct result, to first order in the weak flow field u±​(z,t)u_{\pm}(z,t), hydrodynamic corrections to the static density profile are restricted entirely to the m=±1m=\pm 1 modes. Since the m=+1m=+1 and m=−1m=-1 modes decouple and do not mix, they act as parallel pathways. Drawing an analogy to the signalling framework in Ref. [13], we identify the Y2±1Y_{2}^{\pm 1} harmonic as independent “communication channels” between the cells and the embedding fluid. In this picture, cells generate active stress, injecting a signal of amplitude a2,±1​(z,t)a_{2,\pm 1}(z,t) into the fluid through Eq. (4). In return, the fluid flow reorients the cells, feeding the signal back into the multipole moments al,±1​(z,t)a_{l,\pm 1}(z,t) via Eq. (3). Spontaneous oscillations emerge when the gain of this feedback cycle is positive.

Results– Figure 2(a) displays the real and imaginary parts of χ≡χ′+i​χ′′\chi\equiv\chi^{\prime}+i\chi^{\prime\prime} against ω\omega at ΛT=1\Lambda_{\rm T}=1 and two selected values of Pes{\rm Pe}_{\rm s}. As expected, the imaginary part χ′′​(ω)\chi^{\prime\prime}(\omega) vanishes at zero frequency, as it is an odd function of ω\omega. For the Péclet number Pes=5{\rm Pe}_{\rm s}=5, we observe χ′′​(ω)>0\chi^{\prime\prime}(\omega)>0 for all ω>0\omega>0, indicating that fluctuations are dissipated and the system remains passive. However, increasing the Péclet number to Pes=10{\rm Pe}_{\rm s}=10 drives χ′′​(ω)\chi^{\prime\prime}(\omega) to negative values at low-frequencies. Up to a cut-off frequency ω0>0\omega_{0}>0, the bacterial population develops a phase-leading response to periodic shear flow.

In Fig. 2(b), we show the “active” part of the plane spanned by Pes{\rm Pe}_{\rm s} and ΛT\Lambda_{\rm T}. The orange line separates the region with ω0>0\omega_{0}>0 (shaded) from the passive phase with χ′′​(ω)>0\chi^{\prime\prime}(\omega)>0 for all ω>0\omega>0. The two examples in Fig. 2(a) lie on either side of this phase boundary, shown by the blue (Pes=5{\rm Pe}_{\rm s}=5) and red (Pes=10{\rm Pe}_{\rm s}=10) dots. Active response of swarming bacteria to laminar shear flow occurs only when Pes{\rm Pe}_{\rm s} is beyond a threshold value Pesc​(ΛT){\rm Pe}_{\rm s}^{\rm c}(\Lambda_{\rm T}) (yellow line in Fig.  2(b)). At a given Pes>Pesc​(0)=4.406​…{\rm Pe}_{\rm s}>{\rm Pe}_{\rm s}^{\rm c}(0)=4.406\ldots, the cutoff frequency ω0\omega_{0} for phase-leading response decreases with increasing ΛT\Lambda_{\rm T}, eventually vanishes at the phase boundary.

Spontaneous motion of the bacterial film further requires nontrivial solutions to Eq. (7). Together with Eq. (8), we obtain the minimal cell density c0c_{0} at the onset of oscillations,

c0=−(5​μ​DRσ0)​[χ′​(ω0,ΛT,Pes)]−1.c_{0}=-\Bigl(\frac{5\mu D_{R}}{\sigma_{0}}\Bigr)[\chi^{\prime}(\omega_{0},\Lambda_{\rm T},{\rm Pe}_{\rm s})]^{-1}. (10)

Beyond this density, the torque generated by the cell population is sufficient to overcome viscous forces within the fluid, leading to the elliptical flow as observed in the experiment.

Experimentally, from the balance of the drag force Fdrag∼μ​vsF_{\rm drag}\sim\mu v_{\rm s} with the propulsion strength σ0\sigma_{0}, one may conclude that the ratio μ​vs/σ0\mu v_{s}/\sigma_{0} is a constant, though there could be small variations depending on the bacterial shape and flagellar positions etc. Typically it is expected to fall in the range 0.025∼0.05​μ​m−20.025\sim 0.05\ \mu{\rm m}^{-2}.[16, 5] In Ref.[12], it was reported vs≃34​μ​m/sv_{s}\simeq 34\ \mu{\rm m/s}. Furthermore, their trajectory analysis yielded a time constant τ1=2.3\tau_{1}=2.3 sec for turns of Δ​ϕ>3​π/4\Delta\phi>3\pi/4, which translates to a rotational diffusivity DR=2/τ1≃0.87​s−1D_{R}=2/\tau_{1}\simeq 0.87\ {\rm s}^{-1} when the run direction is randomized upon each tumbling event.

Figure 3(a) shows the minimal cell density c0c_{0} against Pes{\rm Pe_{s}} using Eq. (10) and the experimental parameters given above. The corresponding onset frequency is shown in Fig. 3(b). The translational diffusivity DTD_{\rm T} in Eq. (1) cannot be determined directly from cell trajectories but is usually considered small given the ballistic motion at short times. Remarkably, for both choices of ΛT∼DT\Lambda_{\rm T}\sim D_{\rm T}, the value c0≃0.05​μ​m−3c_{0}\simeq 0.05\ \mu{\rm m}^{-3} is nearly identical to the experimental findings. The onset frequency ω0\omega_{0}, on the other hand, has a strong dependence on the film thickness WW. The shaded area corresponds to the range of WW used in the experiment, where the onset oscillation period is about 44 sec or 0.25 Hz. At a given level of translational diffusivity, the oscillation frequency decreases with increasing film width WW, and vanishes at a maximal film thickness not much beyond 10 μ\mum.

Conclusions — By coupling the dynamics of swimming bacteria with fluid flow through a macroscopic linear response framework, we have elucidated the physical mechanism underlying self-sustained elliptical motion in quasi-2D active suspensions. Our analysis demonstrates that, with a judicious combination of bacterial thrust vsv_{s} and the Jeffery rotation, microscopic active energy is injected to the fluid that manifests as a macroscopic “phase-leading” response to local shear flows. With the fluid flow as the “organizer”, the bacterial nematic stress is able to be channeled coherently to drive the dissipative fluid.

For this microscopic energy injection to trigger a macroscopic instability, three fundamental conditions must align: the cells must respond with the correct phase to amplify the flow, the population density must exceed a critical threshold to overcome environmental viscous damping, and the system must be strictly confined transverse to the flow. The latter aspect is particularly interesting: if the channel width exceeds the typical length of a single bacterial run (effectively lowering the active Péclet number Pes{\rm Pe_{s}}), cells lose their orientational memory before traversing the full length of the film, and thus significantly weaken their coherent macroscopic response. One may also note that, tumbling increases the translational diffusivity DTD_{\rm T} as well, thereby smearing out the polarization profile al,±1​(z,t)a_{l,\pm 1}(z,t) and pushing up Pesc​(ΛT){\rm Pe_{s}^{c}(\Lambda_{\rm T})}. Our work thus elevates the fluid film thickness from a mere boundary condition to the primary control parameter of spontaneous flow. Similar confinement-induced transitions—where boundaries suppress chaotic active fluctuations to stabilize coherent, large-scale flows—have also been established in the broader context of active nematics.[17]

By framing long-range hydrodynamic interactions as a macroscopic communication channel, our model bridges active kinetic theory with the physics of collective synchronization.[13] The excellent quantitative agreement with experimental onset conditions and frequencies strongly validates this first-principles approach. While our linear stability analysis successfully captures the onset of this collective behavior, it naturally leaves the saturated state open. Extending this theoretical framework into the nonlinear regime will eventually clarify the amplitude saturation and long-term topological stability of these emergent orbits, paving the way for a complete thermodynamic description of self-organized periodic motion in confined active matter.
